bib.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 1715-1725

question: Can an NMT model translate rare and unseen words without a back-off dictionary by representing them as subword units, and which segmentation works best?
hypothesis: A segmentation of rare words into appropriate subword units is sufficient for the network to learn transparent translations and generalize to unseen words.
contributions: Open-vocabulary NMT is possible by encoding (rare) words via subword units, simpler and more effective than large vocabularies and back-off dictionaries.
Adapts byte pair encoding (BPE) to word segmentation, giving an open vocabulary through a fixed-size vocabulary of variable-length character sequences.

method.summary: Attention-based GRU encoder-decoder NMT (Groundhog) trained on WMT15 En-De and En-Ru with different segmentations: word-level with or without back-off dictionary, character bigrams with shortlist, and BPE (separate or joint). BPE learns merges over the character-level word frequency dictionary, number of merges being the only hyperparameter.
method.task: neural machine translation (English to German, English to Russian), open-vocabulary segmentation

datasets.name: WMT 2015 English-German
datasets.size: 4.2 million sentence pairs, approximately 100 million tokens
datasets.split: dev newstest2013; test newstest2014 and newstest2015
datasets.source: WMT 2015 shared translation task; primarily parliamentary proceedings and web crawl
datasets.preprocessing: tokenized and truecased with Moses scripts

datasets.name: WMT 2015 English-Russian
datasets.size: 2.6 million sentence pairs, approximately 50 million tokens
datasets.split: dev newstest2013; test newstest2014 and newstest2015
datasets.preprocessing: tokenized and truecased with Moses scripts; Russian transliterated to Latin with ISO-9 for joint BPE learning, merges transliterated back to Cyrillic

models.name: Groundhog attention encoder-decoder (Bahdanau et al. 2015)
models.architecture: bidirectional GRU encoder, GRU decoder with single-layer feedforward alignment model
models.tokenizer: BPE (59 500 merges separate, 89 500 joint) or char-bigram
models.vocab: BPE-60k: 60 000 source/target; BPE-J90k: 90 000 source/target (100 000 target for En-Ru); C2-50k: 60 000

other.fixed embedding layer fine-tune: 12 hours, as suggested by Jean et al. 2015

models.name: WDict
models.architecture: word-level, 300 000 source / 500 000 target vocab, back-off dictionary from fast-align

models.name: WUnk
models.architecture: word-level, no back-off dictionary, UNK for OOV

models.name: syntax-based SMT (Sennrich and Haddow 2015) / phrase-based (Haddow et al. 2015)

training.regularisation: gradient clipping cut-off 5.0 and 1.0 (two independent runs)
training.wall_clock: approximately 7 days, then last 4 saved models (saved every 12 hours) each trained 12 hours more with fixed embedding layer
training.seeds: two independent runs per model (clipping 5.0 and 1.0), 4 checkpoints each = 8 models; seed values not stated

other.objective: inferred: maximum likelihood on parallel corpus with stochastic gradient descent, as in Bahdanau et al.

inference.decoding: beam search, beam size 12, probabilities normalized by sentence length
inference.samples: single system = best of 8 on newstest2013; ensemble of all 8 models

parameters.dictionary_softmax_filter: K = 30000; K' = 10 (fast-align dictionary used for all experiments to speed up translation)

metrics.name: unigram F1
metrics.definition: harmonic mean of clipped unigram precision and recall, reported for all, rare (not among top 50 000 in training) and OOV (not in training) words

eval.protocol: newstest2015 reported; single = best of 8 on dev, plus ensemble of 8; no significance test; authors note up to 1 BLEU variation between models on dev

evidence.quote: also report strong improvements from applying dropout, which we did not use

results.claim: Abstract: subword models improve over a back-off dictionary baseline by up to 1.1 BLEU on En-De and 1.3 BLEU on En-Ru.
results.setup: WMT15 newstest2015, ensembles of 8; the 1.1 on En-De comes from the char-bigram system C2-50k (25.3 vs 24.2), not BPE
results.quote: by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU, respectively
results.note: Table 2: BPE-J90k ens-8 24.7 vs WDict 24.2 = 0.5 BLEU; BPE-60k 24.5 = 0.3. Table 3: BPE-J90k 24.1 vs 22.8 = 1.3.

results.claim: En-De BLEU ensembles: C2-50k 25.3 is best; BPE-J90k 24.7, BPE-60k 24.5, WDict 24.2, WUnk 22.8.
results.setup: En-De newstest2015, BPE-J90k ensemble of 8 vs WDict
results.table: Table 2, row BPE-J90k, column BLEU ens-8

results.claim: En-Ru BPE-J90k gives 1.3 BLEU and 2.0 CHRF3 over WDict.
results.quote:
BPE-J90k yields an improvement of
1.3 BLEU, and 2.0 CHRF3, over WDict

results.claim: Rare-word unigram F1 improves from 36.8% (WDict) to 41.8% (BPE-J90k) for En-De.
Rare-word unigram F1 improves from 26.5% to 29.7% for En-Ru.
German training corpus (about 100m tokens): BPE gives 112m tokens, 63 000 types, 0 UNK on newstest2013; unsegmented has 1 750 000 types.
results.setup: German side of En-De training data, 59 500 merges

results.claim: Joint BPE (89 500 ops) gives 111m tokens, 82 000 types, 32 UNK.
Characters give 550m tokens and 3000 types; character bigrams 306m tokens, 20 000 types.
In 100 rare German training tokens, 56 were compounds and 21 names.
results.setup: rare tokens not among the 50 000 most frequent types

results.claim: Subword ensembles beat WDict by 0.3-1.3 BLEU and 0.6-2 CHRF3.
results.quote:
outperform the WDict baseline by 0.3–1.3 BLEU and
0.6–2 CHRF3

results.claim: Reducing vocabulary and representing more words via subwords can improve performance: C2-3/500k degrades between ranks 50 000 and 500 000 while C2-50k stays stable.
results.setup: En-De newstest2015 unigram F1 by training frequency rank (Fig 2)

limits: Vocabulary size choice is 'somewhat arbitrary, and mainly motivated by comparison to prior work'; optimal size left to future work.
Performance variability: up to 1 BLEU difference between models on dev; single-system numbers are best-of-8 on dev; no significance tests.
No dropout used; Luong et al. (2015a) report 25.9 BLEU on newstest2015 with an 8-model ensemble.
BLEU and CHRF3 disagree on best En-De system (C2-50k by BLEU, BPE-J90k by CHRF3).
Only two language pairs and one architecture (GRU attention RNN, pre-Transformer); BPE-60k suffers from inconsistent source/target segmentation.
Rare and OOV words are only 9-11% of the test sets, so BLEU may underestimate the effect.

terms.definition: learning the encoding on the union of the source and target vocabularies (in practice, concatenating both sides of the training set)
UNK for words outside the model vocabulary, OOV for those that do not occur in the training text
